lines: Blank edges on a map make people braver than they should be.
Every road looks safer when someone else drew it.
The edge of a map is not the edge of the world. It is the edge of our <pulse>nerve</pulse>.
Roads look straight until you have to walk them tired.
Borders are lines people draw so fear has somewhere neat to stand.
A compass helps with north. It says nothing about wisdom.
Most days, I am at the map table, trying to keep roads and borders from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think cartography is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
I trust a good compass more than a loud promise. The compass has less to prove.
A map is a promise with ink on it, and promises need checking.
The edge of a map is never the edge of the world, only the edge of patience.
I trust roads more after they have lied to me once.
Landmarks are helpful because people are very bad at admitting they are lost.
Good ink remembers what frightened feet forget.
A blank corner on a map is not empty. It is waiting to embarrass someone.
You can learn a village by watching which paths people refuse after dark.
Maps do not remove danger, but they make it harder for danger to surprise you twice.
Every road seems honest until rain and panic redraw it.
I mark safe places carefully. They are rarer than people think.
A compass helps, but it cannot tell you why you should go.
The best maps leave room for doubt and better boots.
I have seen straight roads lead people into crooked decisions.
Ink dries faster than certainty. Remember that.
Some places are easier to draw than to explain.
I do not mark every path for every traveler. Some maps are earned.
Keep your voice even. I am measuring more than your words.
Some questions are safer when they stand a little farther away.
I have seen broken cartography with better instincts than you.
That boat route would look peaceful on a map. The lived version was wetter.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.
I could map the route you dragged me along, but I would mark several parts as questionable.
I remember following you through that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across that road taught me to ask more questions before walking.
The ocean crossing by boat would make a fine blue line on a map. I would label it 'questionable judgment.'
That ocean crossing worked because the boat did. I noticed.
The sea made the route look simple. My nerves disagreed.
Maps have edges because paper gives up. The world rarely does.
I mark roads, ruins, and the little places where people decided not to be lost.
A good map tells you where to go. A better one tells you when to turn back.
Most days, I am at the map table, trying to keep roads and borders from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think cartography is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
I trust a good compass more than a loud promise. The compass has less to prove.
I notice when a road bends the wrong way on a map. It bothers me until I fix it.
